The Ares Initiative: six high school students.

We split ARES into parts with shared rules and nearly 700 tests, so we could all build at once. We built it because on Mars help can be 20 minutes away, and astronauts must know before they leave that they can always get home.
summary:
ARES (Astronaut Route & EVA Safety) is a web app that plans safe walks for astronauts on Mars. A planner picks science stops at Jezero Crater, and ARES finds the route that avoids steep slopes and soft sand, budgets oxygen leg by leg, and gives a clear GO, CAUTION or NO-GO before anyone leaves the habitat. A map overlay shows the safe-return zone: everywhere the astronaut could still detour and get home with the reserve intact.

We combined six NASA datasets into one 25 m grid: HiRISE elevation and slope, THEMIS thermal inertia for loose sand, CRISM spectra for clay targets, MEDA weather, RAD radiation, and Perseverance’s real drive path. We used that path to check our map: 99.8% of the rover’s route is rated passable, and our slope tracks the rover’s measured tilt (r = 0.82). A model trained on 31 rover drives chose the same routes as our physics, which supports the cost model.

ARES runs 1,000 simulations of each walk to show the oxygen range at return. During an emergency such as a dust storm, oxygen loss or a blocked path, it re-plans the walk home from the astronaut’s position. “What if” controls show how fragile a plan is. Every number is labelled as observed, calculated or assumed, and any plan can be shared by link or printed as a briefing.

On Mars, help from Earth can be 20 minutes away by radio, so astronauts must know before they leave that they can always make it back.
details:
The problem

When astronauts walk on Mars, nobody can come and get them. A radio message to Earth can take up to 20 minutes one way, so Mission Control cannot guide a walk in real time. The suit carries a fixed supply of oxygen, and the ground is uneven: steep crater walls, loose sand that slows every step, and rocky fields that turn a short walk into a long one. A route that looks fine on a photo from orbit can cost far more oxygen on foot.

The question every surface walk has to answer before the hatch opens is simple: can the astronaut reach the science, and can they always get home? ARES answers it.

What ARES does

ARES is a working web app that plans safe walks for astronauts at Jezero Crater, where Perseverance is exploring today.

  1. Plan: the user clicks science stops on a real HiRISE map of the Jezero delta. ARES finds the route around steep slopes, soft sand and rough ground, then closes the loop back to the habitat.
  2. Budget: it adds up oxygen leg by leg, from walking time on that terrain plus 30 minutes of work at each stop, and holds a 45-minute reserve that the plan is never allowed to spend.
  3. Decide: it gives a clear status of GO, CAUTION or NO-GO, with the reasons written out.
  4. Stress test: it runs 1,000 simulations of the same walk with varied pace and breathing, so the planner sees a range instead of one optimistic number.
  5. React: it triggers an emergency mid-walk (a dust storm, an oxygen leak or a blocked path), and ARES re-plans the route home from the astronaut’s exact position.
  6. Ask “what if”: sliders change the suit’s oxygen, walking speed and reserve, and the whole plan updates instantly.

The demo mission:

  • The plan: three stops on a 4.97 km walk lasting 3 h 35 min.
  • The verdict: GO, with 192 minutes of oxygen to spare. 49% of the oxygen is left at return, and the 1,000 simulations put the 90% range at 43–55%.
  • The storm: a dust storm hits at T+1:16. ARES stops the walk and routes the astronaut home in 57 minutes, arriving with 66% oxygen and still 244 minutes above the reserve.
  • The what-if: if the suit only held 6 hours instead of 8, the same plan drops to a 72-minute margin and turns CAUTION.

A safe-return zone on the map shows everywhere the astronaut could still detour after the last stop and get home with the reserve intact, so the margin isn’t just a number in a panel.

Why it matters

On a future crewed mission, every surface walk will be a trade between science and survival. Planners need to answer “is this safe?” quickly, and they need to trust the answer. ARES is designed as a planning and training aid that makes that answer:

  • Fast: a full plan, simulation and status in under a second.
  • Visual: routes, oxygen, safe zones and emergencies on the real map.
  • Explainable: every number is labelled OBSERVED (measured by a NASA instrument), CALCULATED (worked out by ARES) or ASSUMED (a modelling choice we state openly).
  • Shareable: any plan can be sent as a link or printed as a mission briefing.

The same approach works for any landing site where orbital data exists, and for robotic traverse planning too.

Built on real NASA data
We combined six NASA datasets into a single 25 m grid covering the Jezero delta front:

  • HiRISE DTM and orthomosaic (Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter): elevation and slope (over 25° is no-go), plus the basemap.
  • THEMIS thermal inertia (Mars Odyssey): loose sand that slows walking.
  • CRISM spectra (Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter): clay-bearing science targets.
  • MEDA (Perseverance): temperature through the day.
  • RAD (Curiosity): radiation dose for every minute outside.
  • Rover traverse (Perseverance): ground truth used to check the map.

MEDA and RAD are single-site measurements, not maps. ARES applies them over time rather than pretending they cover the whole area.

We tested it against reality

A route planner is only as good as its terrain map, so we checked ours against the one thing that has actually driven there:

  • Perseverance’s real drive: 99.8% of 20.57 km of the rover’s path is rated passable by ARES.
  • Slope accuracy: at 313 waypoints, our slope layer tracks the tilt the rover itself measured, with r = 0.82.
  • The one failure, reported openly: at Skinner Ridge on the delta front, 41.7 m of the rover’s path crosses ground our map marks as slightly too steep (25.8° against our 25° limit). We show it on the Science page instead of hiding it.
  • Terrain matters: a terrain-blind straight-line route on the demo mission costs 13 more minutes of walking and 18 minutes less spare oxygen. The smarter route pays for itself.

Can machine learning do better?

We also trained a model on 31 real rover drives (15.38 km) to learn how expert drivers actually choose routes, then compared it with our physics.

  • ARES’s physics routes land on average 24.8 m from the drivers’ real path, against 35.3 m for a straight line.
  • The learned model chose the same route as our physics on 31 of 31 held-out drives. That independent confirmation supports our cost model.
  • The safety rule is necessary: without it, the learned model drifts to 27.4 m and starts accepting ground the safety rule forbids, so ARES keeps the physics in charge.

Tech stack

  • Front end: React 19 and TypeScript, built with Vite.
  • Mapping: Leaflet with custom raster layers over a HiRISE orthomosaic, plus a 3D terrain view in Three.js (WebGL) built on the HiRISE elevation model.
    • A* and Dijkstra search on a 25 m cost grid.
    • Leg-by-leg oxygen and radiation budgeting.
    • A seeded Monte Carlo simulator running 1,000 trials per walk.
    • Emergency re-planning.
    • A safe-return zone calculated from walk-home cost fields.
  • Data pipeline: Python with Rasterio for reprojecting and resampling NASA rasters (HiRISE DTM, THEMIS, CRISM), NumPy, and SciPy sparse graph search. It turns six datasets into one 25 m grid.
  • Validation and machine learning: Python scripts that score our slope map against Perseverance’s traverse waypoints and train a learned route-cost model on 31 real rover drives. Charts are made in Matplotlib.
  • Testing: 697 automated Vitest tests, including guards that keep every number in the demo matching the planner’s output.
  • Hosting and tools: Vercel (continuous deployment from GitHub), Git and GitHub, and AI coding assistants, as described in our AI disclosure.

What makes ARES creative

  • It’s a tool, not a picture: most maps show where things are. ARES answers a decision, “go or don’t go,” and shows its reasoning.
  • It checks itself: we validated the map against a real rover and tested the planner against machine learning, then published the one place it fails.
  • It treats uncertainty honestly: simulated ranges instead of single numbers, and every value tagged observed, calculated or assumed.
  • It plans for things going wrong: emergencies and “what if” changes are built into the core of the planner, not added afterwards.
  • It’s built for people: a guided demo, a full-screen user guide with a spotlight tour, plain-language explanations, and a Story tab and a Science tab, so anyone from a student to a scientist can follow it.

Factors we considered

  • Safety first: the reserve is never spent by the plan, and CAUTION and NO-GO always say why.
  • Scientific honesty: we separate measurements from assumptions. Oxygen burn rates are stated as assumptions, single-site data isn’t stretched into maps, and validation results include the failures.
  • Accessibility for judges and the public: one click runs the full guided demo, and every technical term has a plain explanation.
  • Real conditions: radio delay to Earth, storm visibility and slower walking, radiation dose, and time of day.
  • Reproducibility: the data pipeline, validation scripts and tests are all in the public repository.
